1:
Job's great oath of clearing opens not with a protest of deeds but with a bargain struck against the very first motion of sin. The reformed John Gill hears in the covenant Job "made with mine eyes" a solemn engagement not to gaze wantonly upon a woman's beauty, since the eyes are the inlets to many sins, and to uncleanness in particular; Job laid himself under a strong obligation, in the strength of divine grace, to turn his eyes from whatever might ensnare the heart and lead to the commission of sin. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the whole speech under two heads, the lusts of the flesh and the love of the world, the two fatal rocks on which multitudes split, and reads the opening vow as a guard set at the outermost gate: Job would allow his eyes the light of the sun and the glory of God in the visible creation, but never suffer them to fasten on any object that might occasion an impure imagination, much less an impure desire, and that under penalty of penitential tears.

He would not so much as admit a wanton look, nor even a wanton thought, "why then should I think upon a maid?" — for those are not chaste who are not so in spirit as well as in body, and here, Henry marvels, Job understood the seventh commandment better than the Pharisees who sat in Moses' seat, anticipating Christ's own reading of it in Matt. 5:28. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott frames the chapter as one grand profession of innocence, in which Job rehearses his life from the first and clears himself even of sins hidden from other men's eyes, sensual transgression and idolatry, his uprightness the fruit of a rigid and inflexible adherence to principle, the covenant made with the eyes as the very avenues of sinful desire. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps it plain: so far had Job been from any gross wickedness that he abstained from the least occasions and appearances of evil.

Against this near-unanimous reading of chastity, Adam Clarke strikes out alone. Rendering the Hebrew "I have cut the covenant sacrifice with my eyes," with conscience and eyes as the contracting parties and God as judge, the wesleyan-arminian commentator presses the odd word bethulah and proposes that it here signifies not a maid but an idol, the Baithulia or anointed stones of Sanchoniathon and Bochart, animated representatives of a deity, so that Job is purging himself of that species of idolatry from the very first line. The witnesses thus divide at the threshold: is the covenant of the eyes a fence against lust, as nearly all maintain, or, as Clarke would have it, against the worship of consecrated stones? Either way the oath begins where sin itself begins, at the eye.
2:
Having bound his eyes, Job weighs what such a sin would cost, and reckons the loss in the old language of portion and inheritance. The reformed John Gill takes the question as its own answer: what good portion can the impure expect from a God who is above, in the highest heavens, from whom every good thing comes? God himself is the portion of his people in life and in death and to all eternity, but men who live a vicious course can conclude no part in him, nor in his grace, nor any communion with him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry drives the same point through the whole verse: uncleanness is a sin that forfeits all good and shuts men out from the hope of it, for there is no portion, no inheritance, no true happiness for a soul but what is in God and comes from on high; those that wallow in it render themselves utterly unfit for communion with him, become allied to the unclean spirits for ever separated from him, and no unclean thing shall enter the New Jerusalem.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "what then would be the dispensation of Eloah from above, and the inheritance of the Almighty from the heights," and pause here over the singular standing of the man who speaks it. Job is no Israelite, they observe; he stands outside the pale of the positive, Sinaitic revelation, his religion the old patriarchal faith still called in the East din Ibrahim, the religion of Abraham, or the religion of the steppe — a frame that governs the whole self-portrait now unfolding, in which the affliction can neither be squared with guilt nor read as decreed punishment.

The other voices sharpen the sense from their own angles. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, hears in it a note of grievance as well as of awe: though he has not in this or any other respect wickedly departed from God, yet what reward has he received? Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical witness, compares the remonstrance of Joseph, "how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" in Gen. 39:9, making Job's question the same recoil of a conscience that measures sin against the God who sees. And Wesley returns it to the theme of the hidden eye: however secretly the unchaste carry the matter, so that men cannot reprove them, there is one who stands upon a higher place, whence he sees in what manner they act. The witnesses do not divide; they gather around one confession, that the wages of the sin Job has just renounced would have been the forfeiture of God himself.
3:
The question of portion turns, in this verse, into a plain sentence of doom upon the very sin renounced. The reformed John Gill reads "is not destruction to the wicked?" of those who make it their business to ensnare and corrupt the innocent: wickedness of every sort is the cause of destruction, and their wicked ways lead to it and issue in it, even the destruction of soul and body in hell, swift and sudden and everlasting, laid up among the treasures of God's wrath, from which there is no deliverance but by Christ. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same note struck twice, in "destruction" and in "a strange punishment": it is a sin that incurs divine vengeance and will certainly be the sinner's ruin if not repented of in time. Fools make a mock at it, reckon it a peccadillo, a trick of youth, but they deceive themselves with vain words, for because of these things the unsupportable wrath of the eternal God comes upon the children of disobedience, as Eph. 5:6 warns.

Henry lingers over that word "strange." There are sinners whom God goes out of the common road of providence to meet with, and the destruction of Sodom is his instance of a strange and signal punishment; some read the clause as "alienation to the workers of iniquity," and Henry takes both the sin and its penalty in that light — the sin alienates the mind from God, and the punishment is that the sinner shall be eternally set at a distance from him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet as parallel warnings, "doth not calamity overtake the wicked, and misfortune the workers of evil," reading the verse as the general law of retribution that Job's friends had wielded against him and that he now turns to his own guard.

Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, ties the sentence tightly to what precedes: the destruction here named is simply "the portion of" the preceding verse, the negative side of that forfeited inheritance. And Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, keeps the verse within his idolatry reading of the whole passage: had Job been guilty of such secret hypocritical proceedings, professing faith in the true God while in eye and heart an idolater, would not such a worker of iniquity be marked out by a strange and unheard-of punishment? The witnesses converge on the point that matters, that the God Job serves is one whose justice is real and whose vengeance upon the impure is certain, so that the fear of destruction is itself part of the fence he has kept.
4:
Behind the covenant of the eyes and the dread of destruction stands the deeper reason: an all-seeing God from whom no step is hid. The reformed John Gill unfolds "doth not he see my ways, and count all my steps?" of the God who is above and dwells on high, who looks down from heaven and beholds all the ways and works of the children of men. There is no darkness where the workers of iniquity can hide; the fornicator and adulterer choose the night, fancying no eye sees them, but they cannot escape the eye of God, who observes the very methods they take and counts every step, as he reckons up every action of men, good and bad. This, Gill notes, was another argument with Job to avoid uncleanness, for however privately it might be committed it could not be hidden from the all-seeing God — though he adds that some take the words as an appeal or obtestation to God for the truth of what Job has said.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry finds in the verse two distinct things Job had before his eyes. First, God's omniscience: it is a great truth that his eyes are upon all the ways of men, and Job applies it to himself, "doth not he see my ways?" — God sees what rule we walk by, what company we walk with, what end we walk toward. Second, God's observance: he not only sees but takes notice, counting all our steps, all our false steps in the way of duty and all our by-steps into the way of sin, keeping account because he will call us to account and bring every work into judgment. God takes more exact notice of us than we do of ourselves, Henry says, for who ever counted his own steps? yet God counts them; let us therefore walk circumspectly.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott lays the weight on the emphatic pronoun: the "He" plainly means God, and the whole verse is an appeal to the all-seeing knowledge of the One whom nothing escapes, who is judge of the hearts and reins, as in Ps. 7:9 and Jer. 17:10. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, puts the same conviction as a rhetorical impossibility: can Job suppose he could screen himself from the eye of God while guilty of such iniquities? The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's chastity was kept not merely from shame before men but under the constant sense of a divine spectator who numbers every motion, so that the hidden life and the open are alike naked before him.
5:
From the sins of the flesh Job turns to the sins of the market, and swears he has never trafficked in falsehood or hurried after gain. The reformed John Gill weighs the several senses of "if I have walked with vanity": with vain men, keeping fellowship in their sinful practices; or in the vanity of his own mind; or, most likely, using deceitful methods to cheat and defraud, for this seems the vice he now clears himself of, acting unjustly in his dealings and dealing falsely with men. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the plain protest of an honest tradesman: Job never durst tell a lie to get a good bargain, never bantered or equivocated or made many words in his dealings; some men's constant walk is a constant cheat, making their wares more than they are that they may be trusted, or less than they are that nothing may be expected of them, but Job's wealth was not acquired by vanity. Nor did his foot ever haste to deceit; those that deceive must be quick and sharp, but Job's sharpness was never turned that way, and he never made haste to be rich by fraud, acting cautiously lest through inconsideration he should do an unjust thing.

John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, glosses the terms one by one: to walk with vanity is to deal with men in lying and falsehood, and to haste to deceit is, when an opportunity of enriching himself by wronging others offered, to have readily and greedily complied with it. Job disclaims both the settled habit and the seized occasion.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, will not let the honest-dealing reading stand alone, but presses again his idolatrous construction of the passage. "Vanity" here, he argues, renders the Hebrew shav, which elsewhere means a false god, as in Jer. 18:15 and Hos. 12:11; so that "if I have walked with vanity" means if I have been guilty of idolatry, the worshipping of a false god, the whole discourse being to his mind a vindication from all idolatrous dispositions and practices. So a quiet difference runs beneath the verse, whether Job here renounces the cheat's lie in trade, as Gill, Henry, and Wesley take it, or the idolater's false god, as Clarke maintains; but on the ground of the oath they agree, that the man weighed in the balance will be found to have kept truth in his commerce as strictly as chastity in his heart.
6:
Confident of the reckoning, Job flings open his account and asks to be tried by an exact measure: "let me be weighed in an even balance, that God may know mine integrity." The reformed John Gill renders it "in balances of righteousness," the balance of strict justice, God's own justice; Job was so conscious of having done no injustice to any man that, if the weight of righteousness which was the rule of his conduct were put in one scale and his actions in the other, the balance would prove even, with nothing wanting that could deserve a severe censure. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the challenge as the boldness of a clear conscience: Job is willing to have his goods searched, to have all he has gotten enquired into, sure it will be found to weigh well and was not obtained by vanity — for had it been so, then, he says, "Tekel" would have been written on it, weighed in the balance and found too light, as upon Belshazzar in Dan. 5:27. An honest man, Henry adds, is so far from dreading a trial that he rather desires it, assured that God knows his integrity and that the trial will be to his praise.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the forensic edge, taking the whole strophe as a string of self-imprecations governed by this opening wish to be weighed, that God may know — that is, may bring to light and acknowledge — the completeness of Job's integrity. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, fixes the last word: tummathi, "my perfection," the totality of his unblameable life; it is not sinlessness Job claims but the entire and consistent uprightness of his course.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, makes the verse an outright appeal: "I desire nothing more than to have my heart and life weighed in just balances, and searched out by the all-seeing God"; and he reads the second clause not as a wish but as its consequence, "and he will know," for upon such a search God will find out and own his sincerity. So the verse gathers into itself the very image that gives the chapter its temper — a man laying his whole life on the scales of God, not fearing the weight but courting it, sure that when the beam settles it will hang level. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that only a conscience void of offence could ask to be measured by so exact and terrible a standard.
7:
Now the oath takes its characteristic shape, a condition suspended over a curse: if the step, the heart, and the hand have strayed, let the penalty fall. The reformed John Gill reads "if my step hath turned out of the way" of the way of God and of truth and righteousness, so far as Job knew it — for besides the light of nature the patriarchs had some revelation of God's mind — and insists that Job does not claim never to have stepped awry, but that he never knowingly, wittingly, and of set purpose turned out of the way, nor obstinately persisted when drawn aside; and he refers the clause especially to the sin of false and deceitful dealing just renounced. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the three members in turn: Job's steps never turned out of the way of justice and fair dealing, not so much as one step; his heart did not walk after his eyes, that is, he did not covet what he saw that was another's — covetousness being the lust of the eye in 1 John 2:16, as Achan saw and then took the accursed thing; and no blot cleaved to his hands, injustice being a blot to the estate and to the owner that spoils the beauty of both.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch work the grammar closely. "My steps" turn aside from the one right way; the heart goes "after the eyes," following the drawing of the lust of the eye to obtain another's property by deceit or extortion; and a "spot," maum, a macula as in Dan. 1:4, clings to the hands. They note that the offspring here imprecated is not, as elsewhere in the book, the offspring of the body, but, as in Isaiah, the produce of the ground, the very shoots of his fields.

Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, calls the expression emphatic, the narrow way of strict integrity and righteousness, and compares the name given the first believers, the men of "the way," in Acts 9:2. Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, welcomes the scrutiny wholesale — "I am willing to be sifted to the uttermost," for every step of the foot, every thought of the heart, every look of the eye, and every act of the hands; and Wesley reads the heart walking after the eyes as letting the heart loose to covet what the eyes have seen, since commonly sin enters by the eye into the heart, the blot being any unjust gain. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the whole man, foot and heart and hand, is here submitted to trial, and the curse of the next verse is welcomed if any part be found astray.
8:
The condition of the previous verse now discharges its curse: if Job has gained by fraud, let him lose all the fruit of it. The reformed John Gill reads the imprecation straight — should it prove that Job turned out of the way of righteousness, walked after his eyes, and let the mammon of unrighteousness cleave to his hands, then let him sow his fields and another enjoy the increase, one of the very judgments God had threatened against the disobedient. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a man so confident of his honesty that he will forfeit the whole cargo if any contraband be found in it: "let me sow, and let another eat," which was already reckoned the doom of oppressors in ch. 5:5, "and let my offspring, all the trees that I have planted, be rooted out." This, Henry notes, shows that Job believed the sin did deserve such punishment and is usually so punished; yet, though his estate now lay in ruins and at such a time conscience would surely have brought any hidden guilt to mind, he knew himself innocent and would stake the poor remains of his fortune on the issue of the trial.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render it "I will sow, and let another eat, and let my shoots be rooted out," and note that the saying has the ring of a proverb, the same reversal of sower and reaper that lies behind the word cited in John 4:37, "one soweth, and another reapeth." What Job invokes upon himself, should he be guilty, is precisely the frustrated harvest that in the mouth of the prophets is the standing token of a curse.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads the double stroke of the curse — "let me be plagued both in my circumstances and in my family" — and pauses on "let my offspring be rooted out" to observe, from the earlier narrative, that it is probable not all Job's children had perished in the fall of the house in ch. 1:19, so that the imprecation on his "offspring" need not be read against the record. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, simply widens the word "increase" to mean all his plants, and fruits, and improvements, the whole yield of his labour on the land. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job here dares the extremest loss a farmer of the East could name, the seed sown and the stranger fed, as the wager of his innocence in the getting of his wealth.
9:
From his own marriage bed Job turns to his neighbour's, and clears himself of the adulterer's heart and the adulterer's stealth alike. The reformed John Gill reads "if mine heart have been deceived by a woman" of another man's wife, whose beauty might draw a man to lust — and is careful that this was through no fault or artifice of hers, but the danger to which any heart is exposed; yet Job's heart was never so deceived, for he had made a covenant with his eyes not to look upon a virgin, much less upon a married woman, and through the grace of God, like Joseph, he withstood every solicitation, though the wisest of men had his own heart drawn aside by such snares. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the two clauses as coveting and contriving: Job did not so much as covet his neighbour's wife, for the beauty of another man's wife kindled in him no unchaste desire, nor was he moved by the allurements of the adulterous woman of Prov. 7:6; and he never compassed the design, never laid wait at his neighbour's door to seize the chance of debauching his wife in his absence, when the good man was not at home.

Here Henry finds the fountain of all such sin. The defilements of the life come from a deceived heart, he says; every sin is deceitful, and none more so than the sin of uncleanness, which begins in the imagination before it shows in the act. Job's guard, therefore, was set not merely on his conduct but on the secret springs of desire, and it is the inward cleanness, not the outward reputation only, that he here dares to affirm.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the first line "if my heart has been befooled about a woman," and the second of lying in wait at the neighbour's door, taking "neighbour" in the sense it bears in the tenth commandment of Exod. 20:17; Job's heart, they observe, was not persuaded, nor did he give it leave, to trespass upon the marriage relationship of another. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, adds the small textual note that the Septuagint here supplies the words "another man's wife," fixing beyond doubt that it is adultery, not mere fancy, that Job disclaims. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the oath now reaches past the deed to the heart's first consent, and that Job, in the very ruin of his estate, could still protest a marriage bed and a neighbour's door alike undefiled.
10:
To the condition of adultery Job binds one of the fiercest curses in all his oath, and the witnesses divide over just how fierce it is. The reformed John Gill sets out the two readings without finally choosing: some understand "then let my wife grind unto another" literally, of her being put to the meanest drudgery, to work at a mill and grind corn for a stranger, exposed to the insults of the basest of men, as captives were; but others take it figuratively, as an imprecation that she should lie with another and be defiled by him, which is the sense of the Targum and of Aben Ezra, and the following clause, "let others bow down upon her," leans the same way. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry likewise reports both — "let her be a slave, so some, a harlot, so others" — and draws from the harsher construction a sobering providence: God often punishes the sin of one with the sin of another, the adultery of the husband with the adultery of the wife, as in David's case in 2 Sam. 12:11; those who are not just and faithful to their relations must not think it strange if their relations prove unfaithful to them, though the wife's treachery, however God overrules it, is no less her own sin.

The grammatical-historical witnesses render the line and largely take the darker sense. Keil and Delitzsch translate "let my wife grind unto another, and let others bow down over her," and pass at once to the ground of the curse, that this is an infamous act and a crime to be brought before the judges. Charles Ellicott glosses "grind" as performing all menial offices, like a slave, keeping the literal image to the fore.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, gives both a plain and a terrible reading. On the surface, to grind is to work at the handmill, the severe labour of the meanest slave, so understood by the Syriac and Arabic; and "let others bow down upon her" he explains of a bondwoman having no command of her own person, her owner disposing of it as he pleased, as slaves in the East were made to serve even a master's guests. So Job, conscious of innocence, is willing his very wife should be reduced to that indignity if he be found guilty. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, guards the verse from misreading: not as if Job desired this, but that if God should give his wife up to such wickedness, he would own the justice of it. The witnesses do not divide over the horror of the curse, only over its precise edge — the mill-stone or the marriage bed — and Job stakes even that upon his cleanness.
11:
The curse just uttered is now justified by the sheer magnitude of the sin it answers. The reformed John Gill weighs the words "for this is an heinous crime": adultery is contrary to the very light of nature and condemned by it, as well as by the express law of God, and though all sin transgresses that law, some sins are greater than others by their aggravating circumstances. This is one such, a breach of the marriage covenant between man and wife, an injury to a man in what is nearest and dearest to him, and the very thing that brings confusion into families, kingdoms, and states. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry heightens the same note: it is a heinous crime, one of the greatest and vilest sins a man can be guilty of, highly provoking to God and destructive to the prosperity of the soul, and he owns that, were Job guilty of it, both his family and his own person might justly be made a public example.

The clause "an iniquity to be punished by the judges" draws the witnesses to its civil edge. Henry marks that adultery is a crime the civil magistrate ought to take cognizance of and punish, so adjudged even in the patriarchal age, before the law of Moses made it capital — an evil work to which the sword of justice ought to be a terror, and that though the guilty man be himself a judge, as Job was. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the pair "for this is an infamous act, and this is a crime to be brought before judges," keeping the twofold guilt, at once a shameful thing in itself and a matter for the tribunal.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, cites Good's stronger rendering, "this would be a premeditated crime, and a profligacy of the understanding" — not merely a sin against the individuals concerned but a sin of the first magnitude against society, of which the magistrate should take particular cognizance. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, reads the Hebrew as "an iniquity of the judges," a thing belonging to them to punish, even with death, and that not only by the law of Moses but by the law of nature, as the known laws and customs of the heathen nations show. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job reckons adultery no light fault but a capital wrong against God, against the neighbour, and against the whole frame of human society, and would have submitted to a judge's sentence had he been stained with it.
12:
Job caps his abhorrence of adultery with a metaphor of fire, and the witnesses trace the several things it may consume. The reformed John Gill lets the image play over the whole range: it may point to the nature of the sin, a burning lust that inflames the breast; or to its effect, the rage of jealousy in the injured husband, fierce and cruel as devouring fire; or to its punishment in Job's own times, when the Canaanites burned such delinquents; or, most deeply, to the wrath of God, which is poured forth like fire and burns to the lowest hell, into which lake all impure persons will be cast unless grace prevent, a fire that consumes both soul and body in utter and everlasting destruction. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the same senses into one moral picture: "it is a fire"; lust is a fire in the soul, and those who indulge it are said to burn. It consumes all that is good there, the convictions and the comforts, and lays the conscience waste; it kindles the fire of God's wrath, which, if not extinguished by the blood of Christ, will burn to the lowest hell and consume even to eternal destruction, and it roots out all the increase — burning lusts, he says, bring burning judgments, perhaps with an eye to the burning of Sodom.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "a fire that consumeth to the abyss, and should root out all my increase," keeping the double reach of the flame, downward to destruction and outward to the ruin of all a man's substance. The fire that begins in the heart, on their reading, ends in the annihilation of the offender's whole estate.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, brings the image home to the household: nothing is so destructive of domestic peace, for where jealousy exists unmixed misery dwells, and the adulterer wastes his substance on the unlawful objects of his impure affection. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, echoes Henry almost word for word — lust is a fire in the soul that consumes the convictions and the comforts, lays the conscience waste, consumes the body and the substance and roots out all the increase, and kindles the fire of God's wrath which, if not quenched by the blood of Christ, will burn to the lowest hell. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job's judgment that the sin he has renounced is no mere private fault but a devouring flame, destroying the sinner's peace, his estate, his conscience, and, unrepented, his soul.
13:
The oath now moves from the marriage bed to the servants' quarters, and Job swears he never scorned the plea of the lowest in his house. The reformed John Gill unfolds "if I did despise the cause of my manservant or of my maidservant, when they contended with me": whether their quarrel was among themselves, brought before him, he did not reject it for the meanness of the parties but heard each patiently and passed a righteous sentence; or whether the cause was against himself, some complaint of their work or wages, their food or clothing, he did not despise it but searched into its merits. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads Job's whole bearing toward his household as a rare condescension: he did not despise their cause even when they contended with him, but if they contradicted him he was willing to hear their reasons, and if they complained of hardship he did not browbeat them or bid them hold their tongues, but gave them leave to tell their story and redressed their grievances where the right was on their side — a great example to masters to give their servants that which is just and equal, as Col. 4:1 and Eph. 6:9 require, and not to rule with a high hand.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch attend to the wording, noting that the maidservant here is amah, a maid not necessarily a slave, and that the Talmud rightly points out the phrase means not merely that the servants strove with him but that they, on their part, began the dispute — Job did not despise their cause even when they were the ones who raised the contention against their master.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, sets the protest against the harsh law of the ancient world: in those times slaves had no action at law against their owners, who might dispose of them as of their cattle; the master was not compelled to hear a slave's complaint at all. Job's boast is that he had admitted his servants to all civil rights, ready to let them plead even against himself and to give them the full benefit of the law. Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, hears the verse answering a specific charge, for Eliphaz in ch. 22:8 had insinuated that Job favoured the powerful and ground down the weak; Job now meets it, affirming that he regarded his own servants even as brethren, because partakers of a common humanity. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's justice reached below the rank where the age thought justice owed, to the man-servant and the maid who dared to contend with their lord.
14:
Job now gives the reason that held his hand gentle over his household: the thought of a Master above himself. The reformed John Gill reads "what then shall I do when God riseth up?" as the plea of a man who knew that if he had despised or wronged the cause of his servants he would be at an utter loss when God rose to defend it — whether by his providence in this life or at the great day of judgment, when master and servant alike must stand before the judgment-seat and answer for the things done in the body, whether good or evil. Job could frame no excuse, no answer, against that visitation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the same consideration the very curb upon oppression: "if I should be imperious and severe with my servants, what then shall I do when God riseth up?" Job remembered that he had a Master in heaven, to whom he was accountable, who will rise up and will visit, and that we are all concerned to consider what we shall do in the day of his visitation, foretold in Isa. 10:3.

Henry presses the argument home upon every reader. Consider, he says, what would become of us if God should be extreme to mark what we do amiss, should take all advantages against us and insist on all his just demands, should visit every offence and take every forfeiture, should always chide and keep his anger for ever; and, being undone if he were so strict and severe with us, let us not be rigorous with our inferiors. The cries of the injured will be heard, and the sins of the injurious punished; those who showed no mercy shall find none — and what shall we do then?

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence straight on into the ground it rests upon, that the God who will rise up to reckon is the same God who made both master and man. "What should I do," they render, "if God should rise up, and if He should make search, what should I answer Him?" — the question left hanging until the next verse supplies its answer, that the common origin of both binds them as brethren with equal claims. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's mildness toward the meanest of his house was no mere temper of kindness but a discipline of the fear of God, who rises up for the wronged and before whose search no lord of servants can stand acquitted who has trampled on his own.
15:
The unanswerable question of the previous verse finds its answer in a common womb: master and servant were fashioned by one hand. The reformed John Gill reads "did not he that made me in the womb make him?" of God the maker of all: though parents are the instruments of begetting, God is the maker of men, and all, in whatever rank or condition, masters or servants, are alike made by him and fabricated in the same shop of nature, the womb of a woman. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the thought that came seasonably to Job whenever he was tempted to be harsh: "did not he that made me in the womb make him? I am a creature as well as he, my being as derived and depending as his; have we not all one Father?" Whatever the difference of outward condition, of mind or strength or place, he that made the one made the other; and Henry draws the rule of justice from it, parium par sit ratio, let equals be equally treated, for men are all of the same mould, by the same power, for the same end, and so are bound to do to their inferiors as they would be done by.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the grammar of the second line, "did not one fashion us in the womb?" The word "one," they argue, is the subject and means God — unus, the one God who made both, as in Mal. 2:10, "have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" — the reading followed by the Targum, Jerome, and Saadia, and answering to the same thought in Eph. 6:9. They note that others, the Septuagint and Symmachus, construe "one" adverbially with the womb, "in the same womb," but the accentuation and the sense alike favour taking it of the one God who fashioned master and man together.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, reads the verse as Job's steady sense of a coming assize where all civil distinctions fall away: he knew God to be the judge of all, before whom king and subject, master and slave, stand on an equal footing; had he treated his slaves unjustly, how could he stand at that judgment-seat? "I have treated others as I wish to be treated." Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, hears the verse meeting the charges of Eliphaz in ch. 22:6 point for point. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job grounds the rights of the lowest servant not in law or custom but in creation itself, in the one God who formed the great and the mean in the same womb and will judge them by the same measure.
16:
Job turns from his household to the poor at his gate, and answers, article by article, the very charge Eliphaz had flung at him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry recalls that accusation — that Job had withheld bread from the hungry, stripped the naked, and sent widows away empty, in ch. 22:6 and following — and marvels that so positive a charge should prove, by Job's protestation, utterly false and groundless. Job enlarges most on this head, Henry notes, because here he was most particularly accused; and he solemnly protests that he was never wanting to do the poor good to the utmost of his ability, always ready to grant their desires and answer their expectation, so that if a poor man begged a kindness he gratified him, and if he perceived by the widow's mournful, craving look that she looked for an alms though she had not confidence to ask it, he had compassion enough to give it, and never caused the eyes of the widow to fail.

The reformed John Gill measures the protest carefully: Job denies withholding the poor from their desire, that is, from their reasonable desires and such as it lay in his power to grant, as a piece of bread when they were hungry or clothing when they were naked — not their unreasonable or unbounded desires, such as the sons of Zebedee once made, but the honest wants of the needy, which he never refused.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the verse at the head of a long hypothetical period that runs to the imprecation of the twenty-second verse, and render the opening "if I held back the poor from what they desired, and caused the eyes of the widow to languish." The word for the poor man's "desire," they observe, carries the sense of what is ever his interest and his want — the ardent longing of one without means — and Job disclaims ever having denied it. John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, glosses the two clauses simply: to withhold the poor from their desire is to deny them what they sought of him, and to cause the widow's eyes to fail is to wear her out with the tedious expectation of a justice or a charity that never came; and Wesley adds that Job is most large upon this head precisely because in this matter Eliphaz had most particularly accused him. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job answers a slander not with anger but with a plain record of open-handedness, the poor never turned away and the widow's watching eye never left to fail.
17:
Job's charity, he swears, went beyond the alms handed down to a share at his own table. The reformed John Gill notes that though Job kept a plentiful table in his prosperity, he calls his provision a "morsel," and whatever it was, more or less, he did not eat it alone: what he had for himself the poor shared with him, and the same meat he ate he gave to them. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the gesture into a mark of honour done the poor. Job took the fatherless children to eat with him at his own table; they should fare as he fared and be familiar with him, and he showed himself pleased with their company as if they had been his own — for as it is one of the greatest grievances of poverty that it exposes to contempt, so it is no small support to the poor to be respected. He provided them food convenient, Henry adds, and they ate not after him of the crumbs that fell from his table, but with him of the best dish on it, as David took Mephibosheth to eat at the king's board.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the clause forward within the long protestation of Job's care for the helpless, reading the eating of his morsel with the fatherless as of a piece with the clothing of the naked and the guiding of the widow that the surrounding verses recount — the whole a single sustained oath that his bread was never hoarded from those who wanted it.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, sets the custom against the manners of the ancient world, where hospitality was among the most prominent of virtues and the supper the grand meal at which friends and strangers alike were welcome. He derives the very Latin word for supper, coena, from the Greek for communion or fellowship, and quotes Plutarch that the old Romans dined alone but supped with their friends; yet Job, he observes, speaks here of something humbler and better, of dividing his bread with the hungry — for he is a poor, despicable wretch who would eat his morsel alone while another sat by full as hungry as himself. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's table was no private luxury but an open board, where the orphan sat as a son and the stranger as a friend, and that a man's cleanness before God is proved as much by whom he feeds as by whom he spares.
18:
This verse, which grounds Job's charity in a lifelong habit, is at once the most tender and the most tangled in the chapter, and the witnesses labour over both its feeling and its grammar. The reformed John Gill reads it plainly of Job's early and fatherly compassion: from his youth, as soon as he was at years of discretion and could observe the distress of others, the fatherless was brought up with him as with a father, and he acted a father's part to the orphan with a father's affection and care. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expands the same sense across both the fatherless and the widow: Job was a father to the fatherless, taking orphans under his own eye and giving them not only maintenance but education, and a guide to the widow who had lost the guide of her youth, advising her in her affairs and undertaking the management of them; and this from his youth, from his mother's womb, for he had tenderness woven into his nature and his parents had taught him betimes to pity and relieve the poor.

Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, settles the pronouns that make the verse so hard: "he" refers to the fatherless of the preceding verse and "her" to the widow of the verse before that, so that Job says the orphan grew up under his fatherly care and the widow was guided by him from his earliest years. John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, reads it the same way, glossing "from my youth" as from the time he was capable of managing his own affairs, and "her" as the widow already named, guided with all the diligence and tenderness of a father.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, throws up his hands at the sheer diversity of renderings the line has received, and lays them side by side: Heath's "from his youth he was brought up with me as a father, yea, I have guided her from her mother's womb"; Houbigant's "for commiseration educated me from my childhood, and she brought me up from my mother's belly"; Good's startling "behold, from my youth calamity hath quickened me, even from my mother's womb have I distributed it"; Coverdale's "mercy grew up with me from my youth"; the Septuagint's "from my youth I nourished them as a father"; and the Syriac's "from my childhood he educated me in distresses." Having heaped them up, he asks simply, "who can reconcile such discordant translations?" The witnesses divide, then, not over Job's meaning in the main — a life of mercy begun in childhood — but over the wording that carries it; and where the grammatical voices confidently assign the pronouns to orphan and widow, Clarke confesses the line a genuine and unresolved crux.
19:
From feeding the hungry Job turns to clothing the cold, and swears he never let a perishing man go uncovered. The reformed John Gill weighs the words "if I have seen any perish for want of clothing, or any poor without covering": Job does not deny that he had ever seen such cases — men so poorly clad that they were ready to die of cold — but that he had ever seen them so as to "despise" them, to hold them in contempt for their rags, or so as to "overlook" them, to neglect them and make no provision, as the Septuagint and Vulgate variously turn it. To have seen and passed by would have been the sin; Job saw and clothed. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that this care cost more than feeding: the poor may perish for want of clothing as truly as for want of food, whether to lie in by night or to go abroad in by day, and if Job knew of any in that distress he was forward to relieve them. Instead of decking his servants in rich liveries while the poor went in rags fit for the dunghill, he had good, warm, strong clothing made on purpose for them of the fleece of his own sheep.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "if I saw one perishing without clothing, and that the needy had no covering," and fix the force of the participle for "perishing" — one who has come down from his right place and is going to ruin, the very man on the edge of death whom Job's provision drew back from the brink. Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, offers a small alternative to the first word, reading not "any perish" but "any wanderer without" — the homeless vagrant exposed to the weather — so that Job's compassion reached even the stranger with no roof and no cloak.

The witnesses do not divide; they gather around a single picture of a wealth held in trust for the weak. Whether the man in view be the perishing poor or the shelterless wanderer, Job's oath is that he never saw such need and turned his eyes away, but met it out of his own flocks. The clothing of the naked, dearer and less noticed than the feeding of the hungry, becomes in his mouth another weight laid on the even balance, and one he does not fear to see weighed; for the same sheep that were burned with fire from heaven had, while he had them, warmed the bodies of the poor.
20:
The clothing given draws back a blessing, and Job hears it in the very body it warmed. The reformed John Gill reads "if his loins have not blessed me" of the poor man's loins, girded and covered with the garments Job gave, which as often as he put them on and girded them about him put him in mind of his benefactor, and moved him to send up a wish to heaven that all happiness might attend the man who had so comfortably clothed him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same blessing rise: the poor, warmed with the fleece of Job's sheep, blessed him, commended his charity, blessed God for him, and prayed God to bless him. And Henry sets the mercy in the light of Job's later loss — his sheep were burned with fire from heaven, but this was his comfort, that while he had them he came honestly by them and used them charitably, feeding the poor with their flesh and clothing them with their wool.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, calls it a very delicate touch. The part that was cold and shivering is now covered with warm wool, feels the comfort, and by a fine prosopopoeia is made to bless the man who furnished the clothing — the loins themselves, as it were, giving thanks. The figure, on Clarke's reading, turns the gratitude from mere words into something felt in the flesh, the warmth of the poor man's body a silent benediction upon his helper. Gill too had marked that the loins are named because it was there the girdle of the given garment was bound, so that the very seat of the poor man's renewed comfort became the seat of his thankfulness, and every time he girded himself he blessed the hand that had covered him.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the couplet within the running oath, rendering "if his loins blessed me not, and he did not warm himself from the hide of my lambs," and read it as one more clause in the great hypothetical period whose thunderclap of imprecation waits at the twenty-second verse. The blessing of the warmed poor, on their reading, is Job's evidence, offered under oath, that his charity was real and returned in prayer. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job counts as no small part of his integrity the gratitude of the bodies he warmed, the loins of the poor blessing the hand that clothed them, and reckons that blessing, gladly, among the things he is content to have weighed. What in a lesser man might have been a boast becomes in Job an appeal to witnesses beyond himself, the very bodies he warmed rising to speak for him at the trial he courts.
21:
Job now swears he never turned his power against the defenceless, even where power could act unpunished. The reformed John Gill unfolds "if I have lifted up my hand against the fatherless" through its several possible senses: in a menacing way, threatening what he would do — terrible enough from a man of wealth and authority; or to strike, the smiting with the fist of wickedness; or as a signal to others to smite, as Ananias bade men smite Paul in Acts 23:2; or to vote against the orphan wrongly, suffrages being made by the lifting of the hand. So far was Job from any of these, Gill says, that he had not so much as lifted a finger against the fatherless. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays the stress on the clause "when I saw my help in the gate": Job never used his power to crush those who stood in his way, though he had interest enough both in the people and in the judges to do it and to bear him out when he had done it. Those who have it in their power to do a wrong thing and go through with it, and a prospect of gain by it, and yet do justly and love mercy, may afterwards reflect on their conduct with much comfort, as Job does here.

John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, fixes the same phrase in a word: it was "when I saw I could influence the judges to do what I pleased" — the very moment when oppression would have been safe was the moment Job kept his hand down.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, hears in the verse the portrait of a just and open-handed chief, and reaches for a parallel outside Scripture, quoting from Lebeid, one of the authors of the Moallakhat, in Sir William Jones's elegant translation: the desert lord who invites the needy to the slaughtered camel, whose door the worn matron approaches, into whose flowing dish the famished orphans eagerly plunge, who dispenses justice to the tribes, is indignant when their right is diminished, and to establish their right often relinquishes his own. Job, on Clarke's reading, was such a one — able to sway the gate, yet never lifting his hand against the weak whose cause he could so easily have crushed. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's boast is not merely that he did the orphan no wrong, but that he did none where wrong would have gone unquestioned, the surest proof that his justice was rooted in the fear of God and not in the fear of men.
22:
Against the mere possibility of striking the fatherless Job invokes upon himself the loss of the striking arm. The reformed John Gill reads "then let mine arm fall from my shoulder blade" as a wish that the very limb be disjointed and drop off, or rot from the bone — a dreadful calamity, to lose an arm as a judgment from God in just retaliation for lifting it against the weak, as Jeroboam's arm withered when he stretched it out against the man of God in 1 Kings 13:4. And he recalls that Eliphaz had charged that the arms of the fatherless were broken, insinuating that Job had broken them, in ch. 22:9; so Job answers by wishing his own arm broken if that charge were true, an imprecation to be made only when a man's innocence cannot otherwise be cleared, and never lightly or in common. The very boldness of the wish, Gill implies, is itself a kind of evidence, for no man would call down the ruin of his own right arm upon a charge he secretly knew to be true.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the curse the same way and draws out its justice: "let the flesh rot off from the bone, and one bone be disjointed and broken from another"; had Job not been perfectly clear in this matter he durst not thus have challenged the divine vengeance. And Henry finds it a righteous thing with God to break the arm that is lifted up against the fatherless, as he withered Jeroboam's arm that was stretched out against a prophet — the punishment fitted exactly to the offending member.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the imprecation "let my shoulder fall out of its shoulder-blade, and mine arm be broken from its bone," and take it as the delayed apodosis to the whole long series of conditions reaching back through Job's dealings with the poor, the widow, and the fatherless — the single curse under which all those oaths have been suspended. Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, prefers Good's more anatomical rendering, "may my shoulder-bone be shivered at the blade, and mine arm be broken off at the socket," and reads the point of it precisely: let judgment fall on those very parts which have done wrong, or refused to do right when it was in their power. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job stakes the use of his own right arm on his never having raised it against the helpless, a wager no guilty man would dare, and one that answers Eliphaz's insinuation not with a mere denial but with a self-devoting oath.
23:
Job now names the fear that held that arm down: not the dread of men, who were at his command, but the dread of God. The reformed John Gill reads "for destruction from God was a terror to me" of a man who feared not men, since they were at his beck, but greatly feared God — the dread of his resentment, and of destruction from the lawgiver who is able to save and to destroy, so wrought upon him as to deter him from all unkindness to the poor and all injustice to the fatherless. Job feared destruction of himself, his family, and his substance in this life, and, Gill allows, the everlasting destruction of the world to come; and though as one who knew his living Redeemer he might not dread eternal damnation, he certainly feared temporal ruin and the chastening hand of a heavenly Father, for the Old Testament saints were much under a spirit of bondage to fear. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the terror under two heads: the majesty of God, whose highness Job considered — the infinite distance between himself and God, which filled him with a reverence that made him circumspect in his whole walk, remembering that he who is higher than the highest regards, as Eccl. 5:8 says; and the wrath of God, destruction from whom would be certain and utter ruin if he wronged the poor.

Henry draws the standing lesson from it: good men, even the best, have need to restrain themselves from sin with the fear of destruction from God, and all little enough; even when salvation from God is a comfort to us, destruction from God should be a terror, for Adam himself in innocency was awed with a threatening.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, makes the same fear the keeper of his whole life: "I have ever been preserved from outward sin through the fear of God's judgments," knowing that God's eye was constantly upon him, and he could never, in his Judge's eye, his Judge's anger dare. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, glosses the closing clause of standing in awe: Job knew himself unable either to oppose God's power or to bear his wrath. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens that very phrase, correcting "I could not endure" to "I was unable to act thus" — the majesty of God made the wrong itself impossible to Job, not merely its consequence unbearable. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the ground of Job's mercy to men was his terror before God, whose highness overawed him from every oppression his power could have carried out unpunished.
24:
The oath now turns from cruelty to covetousness, and Job swears he never made his wealth his god. The reformed John Gill hears in "if I have made gold my hope" a purging from idolatry in its figurative sense, for covetousness is idolatry and a covetous man an idolater, worshipping his gold and silver, setting his affections on them and his trust in them; to make gold the ground of hope is to set it in the room of God, who is the hope of Israel and in whom every good man should trust. It is not gold on earth but glory in heaven that the good man hopes for, Gill adds, and not riches but Christ and his righteousness that are the foundation of such a hope, which is of things unseen and future; whereas to make gold our hope is to have hope only in this life, and so to be of all men most miserable. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as the first of Job's confessions about his wealth: he had gold, he had fine gold, his wealth was great and he had gotten much, yet he put no great confidence in it and did not make gold his hope. Those are very unwise, Henry says, and enemies to themselves, who depend on it as sufficient to make them happy; it is hard to have riches and not to trust in them, and this is what makes it so difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God, as Matt. 19:23 declares.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears the verse answering Eliphaz directly, who had bidden Job lay up gold as the dust and make the Almighty his defence in ch. 22:23-24; Job replies that such trust in gold had never been his practice, for he had made God, not treasure, his confidence.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, attends to the two words for gold in the couplet, zahab, the polished gold, and kethem, the stamped or standard gold, referring the reader to his fuller note on their difference at ch. 28:15-17, where wisdom is set above them both. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job here renounces the idolatry of the heart that precedes the idolatry of the eye, the worship of wealth that would presently be matched by the worship of sun and moon, and that a man weighed in the even balance must be found to have leaned neither on his gold nor on the shining hosts of heaven, but on God alone.
25:
Having denied that he trusted his wealth, Job denies that he even gloried in it. The reformed John Gill reads "if I rejoiced because my wealth was great, and because mine hand had gotten much" as a disclaiming not of all gladness but of carnal, self-pleasing joy: Job did not set his heart on his riches, nor let them engross his affections or draw them from God his chief joy. A man may lawfully rejoice in God's goodness in increasing his substance, and praise him for it, and cheerfully partake of what is given; what Job renounces is the inordinate delight that terminates in the gift and forgets the giver. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the point: Job took no pride in his wealth, as if it added anything to his real excellency, nor did he think that his own might and the power of his hand had obtained it for him, the very boast that Deut. 8:17 forbids. His joy did not terminate in the gift but passed through it to the giver; in the midst of his abundance he never said, as the rich fool in Luke 12:19, "Soul, take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry," nor blessed himself in his riches.

And Henry finds in this the secret of Job's later patience. Because he did not inordinately rejoice in his wealth, he could bear the loss of it as patiently as he did; the way to weep as though we wept not is to rejoice as though we rejoiced not, for the less pleasure the enjoyment gives, the less pain the disappointment brings. Job's moderate joy in gaining was the very thing that steadied him in losing.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the couplet at the head of the strophe that runs on to the sin of sun-worship, rendering "if I rejoiced that my wealth was great, and that my hand had gained much," and reading it as the covetous counterpart to the idolatry that follows — the heart's over-valuing of gold being of a piece with the eye's temptation to worship the shining hosts of heaven. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job here clears himself not merely of trusting his riches but of the subtler sin of taking his complacency in them, boasting that his own hand had won them, when in truth every increase was the gift of God, held with a loose hand and surrendered without a murmur.
26:
Job passes now from the idolatry of the heart to the idolatry of the eye, and clears himself of the oldest worship of the East, that of the shining lights of heaven. The reformed John Gill canvasses the readings — some take "if I beheld the sun when it shined" of the uncertainty of earthly things, some of ascribing his wealth to the stars' influence, some of Job's not pleasing himself in his prosperity — but concludes, with the general sense, that it means the literal worship of sun and moon, the first kind of idolatry that ever was. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks that Job's friends had not charged him with this, yet there were those in that age so sottish as to worship the sun and moon, else Job would not have mentioned it; it was the most ancient idolatry, the temptation to which was strongest, as Deut. 4:19 warns, though as yet it was practised secretly and durst not appear in open view. Job, Henry says, never beheld the sun or the moon in their pomp and lustre with any admiration but such as led him to give all the glory of their brightness to their Creator; whenever he looked at the lights of heaven he looked by faith through them and beyond them to the Father of lights.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, names the thing precisely: this is Sabaeism, the worship of the heavenly bodies, and the most reasonable and ancient of all idolatries, the sun and moon and the bright planets its first objects. He follows Calmet in finding three things pointed at here — the worship of sun and moon, the custom of adoring the sun at its rising and the moon at her change, and the act of kissing the hand — and traces the very word "adoration" to the Latin for lifting the hand to the mouth. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, agrees that the verse speaks of the worship of the host of heaven, and chiefly of the sun and moon, the most eminent of that number, the most ancient idolatry and the most frequent in the eastern countries, the sun beheld here in its full strength and glory.

The grammatical-historical witnesses render and refine. Keil and Delitzsch translate "if I saw the sunlight when it shone, and the moon walking in splendour," the very stateliness of the images heightening the pull they might have had on a devout beholder. Charles Ellicott makes a shrewd observation: it is remarkable that the only idolatry Job repudiates is that of sun and moon; he seems to have known nothing of the grosser and more degraded kinds, a sign of the pure and primitive character of his religion. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job could gaze on the most glorious works in the visible creation and never let his wonder slide into worship, giving the light itself no honour that was due only to the God who made it.
27:
The oath now follows the temptation inward, from the beholding eye to the enticed heart and the kissing hand. The reformed John Gill reads "and my heart hath been secretly enticed" of the heart drawn away by the magnitude of those bodies, the swiftness of their motion, their glory and usefulness, to entertain the thought of their being deities, and so to worship them privately, by esteem and reverence and trust; for there is a secret idolatry of the heart, an idolatry in the chambers of imagery, as well as an open worship in dark places, such as Ezek. 8:12 lays bare. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two clauses as heart and hand: Job kept his heart with all diligence, that it should not be secretly enticed to think there was a divine glory in the brightness of the lights or a divine power in their influence — for here is the source of idolatry, it begins in the heart, when a man is drawn away by his own lust and enticed, as Jas. 1:14 has it; and he did not so much as put a compliment upon these pretended deities, for his mouth did not kiss his hand, the least and lowest act of adoration.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch dwell on that gesture with antiquarian care. The verb for enticed, they note, is the same as in Deut. 11:16, of a heart giving way to a seducing influence; and the kiss of the hand is a joining of lip to hand in the direction of the venerated object, the proper gesture of the proskynesis or adoratio of the ancients. They cite Pliny, that in adoring we lift the right hand to the mouth and turn the whole body about, and Tacitus, that in Syria men venerate the rising sun — the very rite of throwing a kiss toward the heavens that Job disclaims, kin to the kissing of the calves in Hos. 13:2.

The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as Job's searching of the most secret chamber of the soul, where idolatry is born before it is ever seen. Henry had already traced the whole progress of the sin, from the eye that beholds to the heart that is enticed to the mouth that pays its silent homage; and Job swears that at every stage — the gaze, the inward consent, the outward token — he kept himself clean, giving the shining hosts of heaven neither the worship of his hand nor the far more dangerous worship of his heart. It is the same covenant with the eyes he made at the chapter's opening, now stretched from the lust of the flesh to the lust of false devotion.
28:
Job weighs the guilt of such star-worship and finds it, like adultery, a crime for the bench and a treason against heaven. The reformed John Gill reads "this also were an iniquity to be punished by the judge" of the civil magistrates, God's vicegerents, whose duty it is to take cognizance of an iniquity that so peculiarly touches the honour of the true God — a sin the law of Moses punished with stoning, and which God himself, whose law is broken by it, will visit on the idolater, whose portion is the lake that burns with fire and brimstone in Rev. 21:8. The very heinousness of it, and its sure punishment, deterred Job from it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the two faces of the crime side by side. It is an affront to the civil magistrate, a public nuisance hurtful to kings and provinces, for idolatry debauches men's minds, corrupts their manners, and provokes God to send judgments on a nation, so that the guardians of the public peace are concerned to restrain it. But it is a far greater affront to the God of heaven, no less than high treason against his crown and dignity: "for I should have denied the God that is above" — denied his being as God and his sovereignty; idolatry is in effect atheism, whence the Gentiles are said to be without God, atheists, in the world, in Eph. 2:12.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, puts the theological heart of it in a sentence: had Job paid divine adoration to sun or moon, he would thereby have denied the God that made them — the worship of the creature being the disowning of the Creator. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, reads "the judge" as the civil magistrate, who, being advanced and protected by God, is obliged to vindicate his honour and so to punish idolatry; and he explains the denial as by consequence, not by direct word — to rob God of his prerogative by giving the creature the worship peculiar to God.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises a small question over that judge: he would render it rather "by my judge," meaning God himself, doubting that there is here any reference to the Mosaic law of Deut. 17:2-7. So the witnesses part a little over the tribunal — the earthly magistrate, as Gill, Henry, and Wesley take it, or God the judge, as Ellicott prefers — but not over the verdict; all agree that Job reckons the worship of sun and moon a capital crime, an atheism dressed as devotion, and one he never came near, for to bow to the light would have been to deny the Lord of the light.
29:
The oath now enters the inmost region of the will, the secret pleasure a man may take in an enemy's ruin. The reformed John Gill owns that Job, good man though he was, had his enemies, hated for his very goodness, on whom in time some calamity fell; and it is a common thing with wicked men to rejoice in the adversity of those they hate, but good men should not, though it is a hard thing and requires a large measure of grace in exercise not to feel a secret pleasure at the fall of an adversary. This is the new and searching crime Job purges himself of. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks how far Job kept from revenge: he did not so much as rejoice when mischief befell those who hated him, though many who would not wilfully hurt an enemy are yet secretly pleased and laugh in their sleeve when hurt comes to him. Job was not of that spirit; though there were those that hated him, and evil found them, he saw their destruction and was far from rejoicing in it, remembering that to do so would justly have brought the destruction on himself, as Prov. 24:17-18 warns, "rejoice not when thine enemy falleth."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "if I rejoiced over the destruction of him who hated me, and became excited when evil came upon him," and note the broken construction — an aposiopesis, the sentence left hanging as equal to a solemn denial, to which the next verse attaches its plain negative. The very grammar, on their reading, enacts the recoil of a conscience that will not so much as finish the supposition.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, states it as fact: "I did not avenge myself on my enemy; I neither bore malice nor hatred to him." Charles Ellicott, the second grammatical-historical voice, observes how much deeper Job now searches than his accusers ever did: he proceeds here to the realm of the wishes and the thoughts, and is far more thorough and severe with his own case than his friends had been with it — arraigning not merely his deeds but the hidden movements of satisfaction that a lesser man would never have thought to confess. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's righteousness reached past act and word into desire, so that even the unspoken gladness at a foe's calamity, the commonest and most excusable of secret sins, he could deny under oath.
30:
What Job would not feel in his heart he would not utter with his lips: he never cursed even the enemy whose fall he refused to enjoy. The reformed John Gill reads "neither have I suffered my mouth to sin" of a man who laid an embargo on his tongue, that instrument of so much sin, and kept it as with a bridle from cursing his adversaries or expressing any bitterness against them — a hard restraint when provocations are given, yet one Job maintained, wishing no evil even to his worst foe. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry joins it to the verse before: Job did not so much as wish in his own mind that evil might befall his enemies, never wished a curse to their soul — and curses to the soul are the worst of curses — never desired their death, knowing that if he did it would turn into sin to him; he was careful not to offend with his tongue, as the psalmist resolved in Ps. 39:1, and durst not imprecate any evil, no, not on his worst enemy.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "yet I did not allow my palate to sin by calling down a curse upon his life," taking the mouth here under the figure of the palate, the organ of speech, and reading the verse as the simple negative that completes the broken oath of the preceding line: Job did not rejoice at his enemy's ruin, and — the thought now finished — he did not so much as ask a curse upon his soul.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, states the double abstinence plainly: "I have neither spoken evil of him, nor wished evil to him," and adds the pointed comparison that stings the reader, "how few of those called Christians can speak thus concerning their enemies, or those who have done them any mischief!" The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's forbearance was complete, reaching from the secret wish of the heart to the spoken word of the mouth, so that his tongue, which might so easily have cursed, was kept clean even of the enemy's imprecation. It is one more weight laid gladly on the balance, the innocence not only of the hand and the eye but of the very speech, in a matter where the world would have thought a curse only just. Gill and Clarke alike note how rare such a mastery of the tongue is, and how it argues a heart already schooled in the harder work of forgiveness before ever the lips were tried.
31:
Job calls his own household to witness how far his forbearance toward enemies was tried, and the witnesses divide over just what his servants cried. The reformed John Gill takes "the men of my tabernacle" for either his friends who took a meal with him or, more likely, his domestic servants who dwelt under his roof, and leaves the sense of their saying open. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads it of Job's people so enraged at the enemy who hated their master that they could have eaten him, had Job but set them on or given them leave: "O that we had of his flesh! our master is satisfied to forgive him, but we cannot be so satisfied." It shows, Henry says, how beloved Job was in his family and how heartily they espoused his cause; yet it shows too what a strict hand he kept on his own passions, that he would not avenge himself though he had those about him who blew the coals of his resentment — for great men commonly have such about them, as David had in 1 Sam. 24:4. John Wesley, the wesleyan-arminian, reads it the same way: Job's domestics were so zealous in his quarrel that they protested they could eat their enemy's flesh and not be satisfied, yet he restrained both them and himself from executing vengeance.

Charles Ellicott, the grammatical-historical voice, keeps this construction, glossing "oh that we had of his flesh! we should never be satisfied therewith," and comparing the like impatience of ch. 19:22, so that the flesh longed for is the enemy's.

Adam Clarke, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, turns the verse the opposite way. Following the Targum, he reads it not of revenge but of hospitality: "if the men of my tabernacle have not said, Who hath commanded that we should not be satisfied with his flesh?" — that is, Job's servants had all kindness shown them, lived like his own children, and were fed with the same viands as his family, never seeing flesh come to his table while they were left to live on pulse; and Good renders it likewise, "where is the man that has not been satisfied with his flesh?" So a genuine difference runs through the verse: is it the cry of servants thirsting for an enemy's blood, whom Job held back, as most maintain, or the testimony of servants owning that their master's own meat was freely shared with them, as Clarke and the Targum would have it? Either way, the witnesses agree, the verse redounds to Job's honour, whether for the vengeance he refused or the bounty he kept.
32:
Job closes the roll of his charities where the ancient East set its highest social duty, the welcome of the stranger. The reformed John Gill reads "the stranger did not lodge in the street" of one out of his own nation and far from his country, whether a good man or a bad; such a one Job would never suffer to lie in the street through the night, exposed to the inclemency of the weather, but took him in. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the whole law of hospitality in it: the stranger lodged not in the street, as the angels might have done in the streets of Sodom had not Lot alone entertained them — an instance, perhaps, by which Job was taught, as we are in Heb. 13:2, not to be forgetful to entertain strangers. He that is at home must consider those who are from home, and put his soul in their soul's stead; and Job, noted in his prosperity for good housekeeping, opened his door to the road, keeping the street-door open that he might see who passed and invite them in, as Abraham sat in his tent-door in Gen. 18:1.

Adam Clarke, the wesleyan-arminian, marks how far the kindness reached: not merely to family, domestics, and friends, but to the perfectly unknown and to the traveller passing on to some other district, who found Job's doors ever open to receive them and were refreshed with his bed and his board.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the wording. Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "the stranger did not lodge out of doors, I opened my door towards the street," and read it as the last clause of Job's charities before the oath turns to the confession of hidden sin. Charles Ellicott finds in it the very manners, if not the incidents, of Gen. 19:2-3 and Judg. 19:20-21, where the host presses the wayfarer not to spend the night in the open square; and he notes that "the traveller" is literally the road or the way, that is, the wayfarer who walks it. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's house stood open to the roadside, so that no stranger in his country ever slept in the street for want of a door, and that this open door is the fitting close of a life laid out for the poor, the widow, the orphan, and now the passing stranger — a whole benevolence he is content to see weighed in the even balance.
33:
Job turns to answer the deepest charge his friends had brought, that under a show of religion he had hidden a secret sin, and he does so by naming the first hider of all. The reformed John Gill is careful that Job does not here claim to be sinless — he has owned himself a sinner and disclaimed perfection, and speaks even now of his "transgressions" in the plural — but that he did not seek to cover them as Adam did, palliating and excusing them, laying the blame on his wife as she on the serpent; or the meaning is that Job did not do as men in common do, who through fear or shame endeavour to conceal their sin. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears Job answering Zophar's insinuation that he hid his iniquity under his tongue in ch. 20:12: "No," says Job, "I never covered my transgression as Adam, never palliated a sin with frivolous excuses, nor made fig-leaves the shelter of my shame, nor hid my iniquity in my bosom as a darling I could not part with." It is natural to us to cover our sins, Henry adds, for we have it from our first parents; but he that covers them shall not prosper, as Prov. 28:13 warns, whereas Job, when he had said or done amiss, was always ready to own it and unsay it by repentance.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds here a most evident allusion to the Fall, and unfolds the threefold concealment of Adam — hiding himself among the trees, laying the blame on his wife, and at last charging the whole upon God, "the woman whom thou gavest me"; the spirit of Job's saying is that when he had at any time departed from the path of rectitude, he was ready to acknowledge his error and sought no excuse or palliative for his sin. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, reads it flatly, "as Adam did in Paradise."

The grammatical-historical witnesses weigh the very word.
