Keil and Delitzsch argue strongly for "like Adam" rather than "after the manner of men," since the force of the parallel in Hos. 6:7 lies precisely in comparing the transgression to that of the first man, a like breach of an expressed command. Charles Ellicott holds the question open, rendering "as Adam, or as man, i.e., commonly does," and allowing that there may or may not be here some indication of acquaintance with the narrative of Genesis. So the witnesses divide over whether Job names the man Adam or mankind in general; but they do not divide over his meaning, that whatever his faults, he never played the hypocrite, never buried a cherished sin in his bosom, but brought his transgressions honestly into the light.
34:
Job clears himself next of the coward's silence, the sin of hiding wrong for fear of the crowd. The reformed John Gill reads "did I fear a great multitude?" as a denial: no fear of men ever deterred Job from confessing his fault in the most public manner when conscience convicted him and a public acknowledgment was called for. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes Job's courage the very proof of his sincerity: all who knew Job knew him for a man of undaunted resolution in a good cause, who boldly appeared and spoke and acted in defence of religion and justice, and was never threatened or browbeaten out of his duty. He did not keep silence when he had a call to speak in an honest cause, nor keep within doors when he had a call to go abroad and do good; he valued not the clamours of the mob nor the menaces of the mighty, for the contempt of families never terrified him — he feared the great God, and his curse, not the multitude, and its scorn.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the connecting force: the verse gives the motive Job might have had for hiding his sin, and denies it. He cherished no secret accursed thing, and had no need to play the hypocrite, because he did not dread the great multitude of the people and their moral judgment, nor fear the stigma of the families and the loss of honour in the higher circles, so as to keep himself quiet and retired, never going out of the door.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses read the same courage. John Wesley: Job was a man of resolution, who durst not keep silence or stay within when called to speak or act for God, and was not deterred by the number, quality, or insults of the injurious from reproving them and doing justice to the injured. Adam Clarke asks whether Job was ever prevented by the voice of the many from decreeing what was right, or, when many families espoused a wrong cause, put in fear so as to keep his house lest he must judge against his conscience; and he notes Good's alternative, which turns the verse into a self-imprecation — "then let me be confounded before the assembled multitude" — should Job have done any of the evils just named. The witnesses do not divide on the substance; they agree that Job's open boldness in a good cause, his refusal to be silenced by numbers or shamed by the great, is itself the mark of a man with nothing to hide.
35:
The long defence rises here to its boldest pitch, a cry for trial and a longing that the Almighty himself would answer. The reformed John Gill renders the opening "who will give me a hearer?" — not an idle listener drawn by curiosity, but one to hear his cause and hear him plead it in a judicial way, and above all God himself, to whom Job had all along desired to speak. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a formal readiness to stand trial: "there is my pledge," hen tavi, I bind myself to come into court and abide the issue; O that the Almighty would call the case at once and oblige the adversary to put his accusation into legal form, so that Job might vindicate himself before a judge who would hear him dispassionately; and that his accuser would not indulge in vague charges but draw up a proper bill of indictment, that Job might know to what he had to plead.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the difficult middle clause. Keil and Delitzsch render it "behold my signature — the Almighty will answer me — and the writing which my opponent hath written," taking the word not as a wish that the adversary would write a book but as Job's own mark set to his defence, his subscription challenging reply. Charles Ellicott agrees, "lo, here is my mark," my signature, my declaration which I am ready to subscribe, and "would that I had the book my adversary hath written," that Job might have the indictment in black and white before him and answer it point for point; and he notes that the ordered sequence is here disturbed, the closing appeal of this and the next two verses properly following the imprecation upon his land in the verses after — a deviation, he grants, more natural in some respects though strictly less correct.

John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, reads "that mine adversary had written a book" of a charge given in writing, as the manner was in judicial proceedings, and draws from it the curious inference that Job did not live before letters were in use — the first letters, Wesley supposes, being those written by the finger of God on the two tables; what Job wishes is that his friends, who charge him with hypocrisy, would draw up their accusation in a book. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, so far from dreading a scrutiny, courts it, subscribing his own defence and calling for his accuser's indictment, in the confidence that the more closely his cause is examined, the clearer his innocence will shine.
36:
Job pictures what he would do with that written indictment, and the image is not of dread but of triumph. The reformed John Gill unfolds "surely I would take it upon my shoulder" three ways: he would take up the charge as a light thing, having nothing weighty in it; or he would bear it openly, confessing whatever it justly proved; but rather he would carry it as an honour, as a man bears a sceptre or the sword of state upon his shoulder, not doubting the trial would turn to his glory — and so too he would bind it as a crown to him. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears in the whole passage a trial moved for and eagerly pressed: an upright heart does not dread a scrutiny, and Job would be pleased with the indictment and look on it as his ornament; for if it discovered to him any sin he had not seen, he would be glad to know it, that he might repent; and if it charged him falsely, he doubted not to disprove it, so that his innocence would be cleared as the light and he come off with the more honour.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "truly I will carry it upon my shoulder, I will wind it about me as a crown," and carry the confidence straight into the next verse, where Job would recount the number of his steps and draw near to God as a prince — the bearing throughout that of a man sure of acquittal.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke enriches the picture from the customs of the East and beyond. He would be content, Clarke says, to stand before the bar as a criminal bearing on his shoulder the board to which the accusation was affixed — and he points to a book of Chinese punishments before him, in which the crime is written on a board or heavy plank fitted about the offender's neck, to be carried about for the length of his punishment. Job, far from counting this a disgrace, would clasp it as dearly as a crown, being assured that at his trial his innocence would fully appear; and Clarke adds that in the East a favour received from a superior is at once placed upon the head as a mark of respect. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job would wear his very indictment as a diadem, so certain is he that the charge, once weighed, would prove his honour and not his shame.
37:
Job would meet his judge not as a cowering prisoner but as a prince rendering his account. The reformed John Gill reads "I would declare unto him the number of my steps" of a man ready to give his judge a full narrative of his life, all its transactions so far as he could remember — not that God stands in need of such a declaration, for he compasses all our paths, but to show how confident Job was of his innocence and how little he feared the closest examination of his ways. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the defendant ready to make his appearance and give his accusers all the fair play they could ask: he will declare the number of his steps, let them into the whole history of his life, what made against him as well as what made for him — and so confident is he of his integrity that, as a prince to be crowned rather than a prisoner to be tried, he would go near to God, both to his accuser to hear the charge and to his judge to hear the sentence.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it likewise of a man who would show his adversary every station and office of his life, that his whole course might be traced, and would go into the presence of his judge as the nagid, the chief or sovereign commander, not shrinking from investigation by even the meanest of his people; and he gathers the passage into a fivefold desire — that Job be brought to trial, that his accusers reduce their charge to writing, that the Almighty and not man be judge, that Job might cheerfully confess all his ways, and that he might thus go boldly before him. John Wesley glosses the terms briefly: "him" is Job's judge or adversary, "my steps" the whole course of his life, and "as a prince" with undaunted courage and confidence.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott owns that the exact sense is uncertain: Job would either readily give an account of all his actions and meet God with alacrity and perfect confidence, or meet him as one would meet a prince, with the utmost deference and honour, not as an enemy. And Ellicott sets against Job's noble self-assurance the long roll of names his friends had flung at him — a fool, a man full of words, a liar and a mocker, perverse and wicked, a blasphemer and a hypocrite, a robber and an oppressor. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job, arraigned by men as the vilest of sinners, would draw near to God with the bearing of a prince, so clear was the conscience on which he staked his cause.
38:
Job closes his oath where a landholder's guilt would first be seen, in the very ground he tilled, and the witnesses note at once that the verse seems to stand out of its place. The reformed John Gill observes that some would move these closing verses earlier, but keeps them where all copies set them, and reads Job returning, after his appeal to the judge, to clear himself of one last public sin, tyranny and oppression: he denies that the land he owned cried out against him as unjustly gotten, by fraud or force, or as ill-used and never suffered to rest. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the verse as Job's clearing from oppression and violence: his estate was both got and used honestly, so that his land could not cry out against him nor its furrows complain, as they do against those who gain possession by fraud and extortion, over whom the very stone cries out of the wall in Hab. 2:9-11. The whole creation groans under man's sin, Henry says, but land unjustly held cries out against its holder, accuses and condemns him, and demands justice.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke states plainly that the introduction of these three verses here disturbs the connection and that they are evidently out of their place; he refers Job's meaning to the law of the land's sabbath in Lev. 25:1-7, and reads Job as conscious that he had not exhausted the soil by perpetual cultivation, so that his land could not cry against him nor its furrows complain.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the second line more strongly, "or if the furrows thereof weep together," a bold impersonation of the wrong done by oppression, and draws the larger point: throughout this defence Job has far more than traversed the indictment of his friends, showing himself not merely innocent of the moral law's breach they insinuated but exemplary in all the relations of life, so that he was, as the narrator says, one that feared God and eschewed evil, perfect and upright. John Wesley reads the cry of the land simply, "because I have gotten it by fraud or violence." The witnesses divide only over the verse's place — Clarke holding it displaced and belonging earlier, Gill keeping the received order — but agree in its sense, that Job's very fields, had they been wrung from others or worn out by greed, would have found a voice against him, and that they had none.
39:
Job spells out the two ways a man might wrong his land, and denies them both. The reformed John Gill reads "if I have eaten the fruits thereof without money" of a man who ate nothing of his land's increase without having paid for it — who had not got his fields by deceit or violence from their rightful owners, nor failed to pay the labourers who ploughed and reaped, nor taken the fruits from his tenants without a proper price. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry names the two things Job could safely say of his estate: that he never ate its fruits without money, but paid for what he purchased, as Abraham paid for the field in Gen. 23:16 and David for his threshingfloor in 2 Sam. 24:24, and gave his labourers their due wages; and that he never caused the owners to lose their life, never got an estate as Ahab got Naboth's vineyard, by killing the heir and seizing the inheritance, nor starved his tenants with hard usage.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same double innocence: Job was never that narrow-minded man who, out of covetousness, exhausts his land and puts himself to no charge of labour and manure, nor one who defrauds those employed under him of their wages; if he ate the fruits, he had cultivated the soil at his own expense and paid the workers. And he notes Coverdale's turn of the second clause, "if I have grieved any of the plowmen," for they never laboured for him without their due recompense. John Wesley glosses the verse briefly: to eat the fruits without money is either not to pay the price of the land or to defraud the workmen of their wages, and to cause the owners to lose their life is to kill them, that Job might have undisturbed possession, as Ahab did to Naboth.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet "if I have devoured its strength without payment, and caused the soul of its possessor to expire," and add the solemn editorial note that here "the words of Job are ended." The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's last oath touches the getting and the holding of his land, and that he could swear his fields were come by honestly, his workmen paid, and no man's blood or livelihood spent to enlarge them — the final weight laid on the balance before the great self-defence falls silent.
40:
The oath ends as it has run throughout, with a curse invoked upon the head of guilt, and then the narrator's quiet epitaph on the whole speech. The reformed John Gill reads the imprecation straight: if Job's land was unjustly gained or ill-used, let thistles grow where he sowed wheat and noxious weeds where he sowed barley, an echo of the original curse upon the ground, and a judgment God does sometimes execute, turning a fruitful land into barrenness for the wickedness of those who dwell in it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same self-imprecation and draws the moral: when men get estates unjustly they are justly deprived of the comfort of them and disappointed of their expectations, for what was sown wheat comes up thistles, and what men do not come honestly by will never do them good. And on the closing words, "the words of Job are ended," Henry marks that Job has now said all he would say in his own defence — he would afterward speak in self-abasement, but here ends his vindication — and he closes it, some think, with an air of assurance and triumph, keeping the field and doubting not to win it: "who shall lay anything to the charge of God's elect? It is God that justifieth," as Rom. 8:33 declares.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke works at the two rare plant-names — the choach he takes for some hooked thorn or brier, and the boshah for a fetid, poisonous weed, perhaps the nightshade or the aconite that grows rank among the vineyards of the East — so that Job wishes such a crop instead of barley if he has wronged either his land or his labourers.

Clarke lingers longest over the last sentence. "The words of Job are ended," he notes, means the end of his defence against his friends; he spoke afterward, but only to God, who came to determine the whole controversy. Clarke judges the clause itself to be very like an addition by a later hand, wanting in many manuscripts of the Vulgate and standing detached in the Hebrew, so that Coverdale set it off in a separate line, "Here end the words of Job," as one closes a chapter or a lesson. He follows Kennicott too in reading the great appeal of the preceding verses as the true climax, a man conscious of innocence wishing God himself to draw the indictment, that he might bind it as a crown and advance to trial with the dignity of a prince. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that Job's long self-defence closes on a note of settled confidence, the last curse invoked and the last word spoken, a man who has laid his whole life on the balance and is content to leave the beam to settle in the hand of God.
